## Setup
```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidytext)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)
library(tibble)
library(scales)
```
# Part I

```{r}
# You will need the correct file paths if you don't follow my naming conventions:
file_a <- "texts/A07594__Circle_of_Commerce.txt"
file_b <- "texts/B14801__Free_Trade.txt"

# Read the raw text files into R
text_a <- read_file(file_a)
text_b <- read_file(file_b)

# Combine into a tibble for tidytext workflows
texts <- tibble(
  doc_title = c("Text A", "Text B"),
  text = c(text_a, text_b)
)

texts
```

```{r}
# Start with tidytext's built-in stopword list
data("stop_words")

# Add our own project-specific stopwords (you can, and will, expand this list later)
custom_stopwords <- tibble(
  word = c(
    "vnto", "haue", "doo", "hath", "bee", "ye", "thee"
  )
)

all_stopwords <- bind_rows(stop_words, custom_stopwords) %>%
  distinct(word)

all_stopwords %>% slice(1:10)
```

```{r}
words <- texts %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text)
corpus_diagnostics <- words %>%
  group_by(doc_title) %>%
  summarise(
    total_tokens = n(),
    tokens_after_stopwords = sum(!word %in% all_stopwords$word),
    tokens_removed = total_tokens - tokens_after_stopwords,
    percent_removed = tokens_removed/total_tokens * 100
  )
corpus_diagnostics
```
1. 56.6% of Text A and 59.8% of Text B are removed as stopwords. The percentages are approximately the same. Since the removal of the stopwords accounts for more than half of tokens, I'll say stopword removal does greatly affect the texts we analyze. It greatly decrease the amount of tokens we need to work on by deleting those words that may not have actual meanings.

# Part II

## Before Stopword Removal

```{r}
word_counts_1 <- texts %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  mutate(word = str_to_lower(word)) %>%
  count(doc_title, word, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r}
plot_n_words <- 15  # you can change this as needed

# Select the most frequent words overall
word_comparison_tbl <- word_counts_1 %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = doc_title,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(max_n = pmax(`Text A`, `Text B`)) %>%
  arrange(desc(max_n))

word_plot_data <- word_comparison_tbl %>%
  slice_head(n = plot_n_words) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Text A`, `Text B`),
    names_to = "doc_title",
    values_to = "n"
  ) %>%
  mutate(word = fct_reorder(word, n, .fun = max))

ggplot(word_plot_data, aes(x = n, y = word)) + #black magic happens thanks to ggplot
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ doc_title, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Most frequent words (before stopword removal)",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Top ", plot_n_words,
      " words by maximum frequency across both texts"
    ),
    x = "Word frequency",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## After Stopword Removal

```{r}
word_counts_2 <- texts %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  mutate(word = str_to_lower(word)) %>%
  anti_join(all_stopwords, by = "word") %>%
  count(doc_title, word, sort = TRUE)
word_counts_2
```

```{r}
plot_n_words <- 15  # you can change this as needed

# Select the most frequent words overall
word_comparison_tbl <- word_counts_2 %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = doc_title,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(max_n = pmax(`Text A`, `Text B`)) %>%
  arrange(desc(max_n))

word_plot_data <- word_comparison_tbl %>%
  slice_head(n = plot_n_words) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Text A`, `Text B`),
    names_to = "doc_title",
    values_to = "n"
  ) %>%
  mutate(word = fct_reorder(word, n, .fun = max))

ggplot(word_plot_data, aes(x = n, y = word)) + #black magic happens thanks to ggplot
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ doc_title, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Most frequent words (stopwords removed)",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Top ", plot_n_words,
      " words by maximum frequency across both texts"
    ),
    x = "Word frequency",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
2. Before stopword removal, the word 'the' dominates the frequency results, and the other frequent words are also articles, prepositions, and conjunctions. After stopword removal, we get to see words like 'trade', 'exchange', and 'merchants', basically words that contain more specific meanings. Thus, I do believe removing stopwords make it easier to understand the texts of the subject matter. For instance, you can tell that the two texts are both are about business related things through the high frequency of 'trade' or 'money'. Without removal, we can tell nothing from 'the' or 'and'. However, deleting stopword might weaken the connection between different words, because now we cannot tell how different tokens are connected to each other (For instance, are two words connected using 'and' or 'of'? The difference could have different meanings).

# Part III

```{r}
word_counts_3 <- texts %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  mutate(word = str_to_lower(word)) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  count(doc_title, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)
word_counts_3
```
Final Reflection: Words like haue, hath, bee appeared among the frequent words before the custom stopword list was applied. These words are meaningless and have no effects on understanding the subject matter because they have no correlation to those words that we care about (like 'merchant' or 'trade'). However, if we want to do research on historical spelling variants, then these words are strongly correlated to what we are interested in. In that case, they should not be removed. Afterall, there is no universal 'correct' stopword list because different stopword lists are created for different purposes. That's why even if we are analyzing the same article, the stopword list can be completely different based on what kind of words we want our tokens to contain.
